label: Rules & Safeguarding
blurb: Discipline, reporting duties, gender equity, bullying and privacy. Read these through — they are not drilled, because knowing them has to be reliable, not lucky.
blurbZh: 管教、通報義務、性平、霸凌與個資。這幾塊請完整讀過——它們不做每日抽考，因為這種知識必須是可靠的，不能靠剛好被抽到。

questions.stem: Zero corporal punishment in Taiwanese schools is established by:
options: Individual school policy, which varies between schools
Ministry of Education advice that schools may adopt
Statute — Article 8 of the Educational Fundamental Act
A collective agreement between teachers' associations
questions.why: Article 8 of the Educational Fundamental Act (教育基本法) protects students' right to bodily autonomy and to the development of their personality, and requires that they suffer no corporal punishment or bullying. Taiwan banned corporal punishment in schools in 2006. This is law, not local preference — no principal can authorize an exception.

questions.stem: A class is noisy, so you make them do twenty press-ups. This is:
options: Acceptable — it is exercise, not punishment
Acceptable if you join in
Capable of being corporal punishment, because requiring physical exertion or positions as a penalty is covered
Acceptable for older students only
questions.why: The definition covers requiring a student to hold or perform particular physical actions for the purpose of punishment, where the student objectively suffers physical pain or harm. Press-ups, laps, squats, kneeling and holding arms out all fall in scope. “It's just exercise” is the most common misunderstanding in this module, and intent to be harsh is not required.

questions.stem: Standing reflection (站立反省) is permitted, but with what limits?
options: No more than one class period at a time, and no more than two hours cumulatively in a day
No more than ten minutes, once per week
No limits, provided the student can see the board
It is not permitted at all
questions.why: The Ministry's guidance permits standing reflection expressly, capped at one class period per instance and two hours in total per day. Beyond those limits it stops being a permitted measure and becomes corporal punishment. Knowing the cap is what makes the measure safely usable.

questions.stem: Which of these is on the list of permitted general disciplinary measures?
options: Keeping the whole class in because one student misbehaved
Lowering a student's grade for talking
Making a student kneel at the front
Requiring a written self-reflection
questions.why: A verbal apology or written self-reflection is expressly permitted. The others are not: collective punishment is not on the list, kneeling is a physical position imposed as a penalty, and behavior must not be punished through academic marks. A reliable working rule — if it is not on the list, do not reach for it.

questions.stem: You want a student to stay after school to finish work. What is required?
options: Nothing; it is within your normal authority
The homeroom teacher's agreement only
The guardian's consent
A written request to 教務處
questions.why: After-school detention requires the guardian's consent. Practically this means it is arranged through the homeroom teacher, who has the family contact — never keep a student back on your own initiative. A child who misses their ride or their after-school class creates a problem far larger than the one you were solving.

questions.stem: A student scores badly on a test. May you impose a punishment for the result?
options: No — academic results are not a behavior matter
Yes, if the student clearly did not prepare
Yes, if the parents have agreed to it
Only for repeated poor results
questions.why: Punishing a student because of academic performance is outside the purpose of the guidance, which is about behavior and guidance rather than results. Poor performance is a teaching problem and sometimes a welfare signal — if you are worried, that concern belongs with the homeroom teacher or 輔導室.

questions.stem: A student is using a phone in your lesson. What may you do?
options: Keep it until the end of the week so the lesson is learned
Hand it to another student for safekeeping
Delete anything inappropriate on it before returning it
Hold it for the remainder of the lesson and return it; anything longer goes through 學務處
questions.why: You may temporarily hold an item that is disrupting the lesson, but it must be returned, and anything beyond the end of the lesson should go through 學務處. Never keep a phone overnight, never hand it to another student, and never look through its contents — that last one is a privacy problem of an entirely different order.

questions.stem: Two students start fighting. What is your role?
options: Protect the other students, call for help at once, and remove a student from the scene only if there is a risk to someone's life or body
Send the whole class out and deal with it alone
Wait outside the room until it stops
Physically separate them yourself immediately
questions.why: Where there is a risk of harm to another person's life or body, a student may be removed from the scene and outside help sought. But your first job is the other thirty students and raising the alarm — not becoming the adult who wrestles a teenager, which is how a discipline incident becomes an incident about you. Send a student to the office if you have no other way to call for help.

questions.stem: You ask 學務處 for urgent help with a situation you cannot contain. Under the February 2024 amendment:
options: They must first obtain the principal's approval
They may decline if they are short-staffed
They cannot refuse a teacher's request for assistance in an urgent situation
The request must be made in writing
questions.why: The 2024 amendment made explicit that Student Affairs and Counseling cannot refuse a teacher's request for help when the situation is urgent. Worth knowing: it means asking for help is a right you are exercising, not a favor you are requesting — and not a signal that you cannot manage your class.

questions.stem: A student will not move seats when asked. You take hold of their arm to move them. This is:
options: Fine, since no harm was intended
Not permitted — physical force is prohibited outside the genuine safety exception
Fine, because seating changes are a permitted measure
Fine if the student is small
questions.why: Adjusting seating is a permitted measure; applying physical force to achieve it is not. The exception is a real risk to someone's life or body, which a refusal to move seats is not. When a student will not comply, the answer is your co-teacher or the homeroom teacher — not your hands.

questions.stem: Which of these is the clearest breach of the principle of respecting student dignity?
options: Moving a student to the front of the room
Mocking a student's ability in front of the class
Asking a student to write a reflection
Telling the homeroom teacher about repeated lateness
questions.why: Respect for the student's dignity is a stated principle of the guidance. Public mockery, remarks about a student's intelligence, and comments about their family are not discipline — and unlike a physical breach, this one tends to be witnessed by thirty people who will describe it accurately later.

questions.stem: Where does a foreign English teacher's real influence over classroom behavior mainly come from?
options: The relationship with the class, lesson design, seating, and a co-teacher who can intervene in Chinese
The threat of contacting parents directly
The ability to report students to 學務處
Formal disciplinary authority within the school system
questions.why: You generally hold no formal disciplinary authority, and that matters far less than it sounds. Design, seating, relationship and a co-teacher who can say in three seconds of Chinese what takes you five minutes of English will settle more classes than any sanction available to you.

questions.stem: What is the correct escalation order for a persistent behavior problem?
options: Straight to 學務處, so it is documented from the start
Handle it yourself → co-teacher → homeroom teacher (導師) → 學務處
Contact the parents yourself, then the homeroom teacher
Wait until it resolves itself
questions.why: Going straight to the office for small things spends credibility you will want for something serious; never escalating at all is how a class becomes unteachable by March. The 導師 is the pivotal step — they hold the relationship with the student and the family that you do not.

questions.stem: You lose your temper and shout at a class in a way you immediately regret. What is the best next step?
options: Say nothing and hope it is not mentioned
Apologize to the class the following week
Tell your co-teacher the same day, in your own words
Explain yourself to the principal in writing
questions.why: A teacher who reports their own bad moment is a colleague having a bad day. The identical event, first described by a student to a parent three days later, is something else entirely — and by then you are responding rather than explaining. Same day, own words, to the person who works alongside you.

questions.stem: Corporal punishment in the Taiwanese definition means:
options: Hitting a student, and nothing else
Any punishment a student dislikes
Only punishment that leaves a visible mark
Applying physical force, or requiring physical positions or exertion, as a punishment causing pain or harm
questions.why: The definition is functional and broader than hitting: force applied by the teacher, force the teacher has the student or a third party apply, or being made to hold or perform physical actions, for the purpose of punishment, causing objective pain or bodily or mental harm. The second clause is the one that catches teachers who never intended anything of the kind.

questions.stem: Which of these may you do on your own initiative in an English lesson?
options: Contact the student's parents directly
Change a student's seat
Send a student home
Keep a student after school
questions.why: Seating changes are yours to make and are one of the most effective tools you have. Detention needs the guardian's consent, sending a student home is not yours to decide, and family contact goes through the homeroom teacher rather than direct from you.

questions.stem: Who is usually the most effective person to involve when one student's behavior keeps disrupting your lesson?
options: The homeroom teacher 導師
The principal
The Personnel Office
Another student's parent
questions.why: The 導師 stays with that class for years, knows the student's home situation, and is the family's contact. They can often change in one conversation what you cannot change in a term — and they would rather hear it from you early than discover it late.

questions.stem: Your class is loud, so you keep everyone in during their break. This is:
options: A standard and permitted measure
Permitted once per semester
Permitted if the whole class was in fact noisy
Not on the list of permitted measures — collective punishment for one student's behavior is not an accepted approach
questions.why: Collective punishment does not appear among the permitted general measures, and the working rule holds: if it is not on the list, do not reach for it. It also reliably damages your relationship with the students who behaved, who are the ones you most need on your side.

questions.stem: You are struggling to manage a class and feel you should handle it alone to avoid looking incompetent. Which is true?
options: In urgent situations 學務處 and 輔導室 cannot refuse a request for help — asking is normal practice, not an admission
You should only ask after a term of trying
Asking for help will be noted as a weakness
Foreign teachers are expected to manage without support
questions.why: The 2024 amendment makes explicit that help cannot be refused in urgent situations, which tells you how the system regards asking. Colleagues here ask each other constantly; the teacher who visibly struggles alone for a term is the one who worries people.

questions.stem: During a co-taught lesson, your co-teacher raps a student's knuckles with a ruler. What is the right response?
options: Say nothing; discipline in her lesson is her business
Challenge her about it immediately, in front of the class
Ask other students afterwards whether this happens often
Say nothing in the room, then raise it with 學務處 or the principal the same day — and if the child appears hurt, the Module 4 duty also applies
questions.why: Confronting a colleague in front of students helps nobody and makes the situation about the two of you. But this is not something you can leave alone either: schools have a formal process for investigating suspected improper discipline, and it starts with someone telling them. Do not canvass students — that contaminates any investigation. If the child appears to have been hurt, the reporting duty from Module 4 runs in parallel and on its own 24-hour clock.

questions.stem: You raise a difficult class with the homeroom teacher, who says: “You just need to be stricter.” What is the most productive response?
options: Accept it and impose harsher sanctions
Ask her to sit in on one lesson and tell you what she sees, and ask which specific students to focus on
Escalate to 學務處 over her head
Conclude that no support is available and manage alone
questions.why: “Be stricter” is usually shorthand for “I don't have a specific picture of what is happening in your room.” Asking her to observe converts vague advice into concrete information and quietly makes her a stakeholder in the outcome. It also puts a Chinese-speaking adult with authority in the room, which frequently changes the class by itself.

questions.stem: A parent complains that you humiliated their child in front of the class. You believe you simply corrected the student. What should you do first?
options: Respond to the parent directly with your account
Wait to see whether the school raises it
Ask the class to confirm your version
Write down what happened while you remember it, and tell your co-teacher and the homeroom teacher today
questions.why: Get your account written and into the school's hands the same day, before the version traveling through the parent network becomes the only one on record. Do not reply to the parent yourself — that is the school's channel — and never ask students to back you up, which turns a manageable complaint into something that looks like pressuring witnesses.

questions.stem: You are asked to supervise a punishment — a group of students running laps for misbehaviour. You think it may be corporal punishment. What do you do?
options: Supervise it, since a Taiwanese colleague decided it
Refuse loudly in front of the students
Do not supervise it; say privately that you understand physical exertion as a penalty to be covered by the prohibition, and ask 學務處 to confirm
Supervise it but report it afterwards
questions.why: Supervising it makes you a participant, and “someone senior told me to” will not help afterwards. Refusing in front of students costs your colleague face for no benefit. Decline quietly, put it as a question about the rule rather than an accusation about them, and let 學務處 give the answer — asking for confirmation is a normal thing a careful teacher does.

questions.stem: A student blocks the doorway and refuses to let you leave the room at the end of a lesson. What is the correct response?
options: Physically move the student aside — you are entitled to leave
Stay calm, do not touch the student, call or send for help, and let a colleague resolve it
Wait silently until the student gives up
Threaten to call the police
questions.why: Nothing here meets the genuine safety exception, so laying hands on the student converts a manageable moment into an incident about you — with witnesses. Stay calm, keep distance, get another adult. In urgent situations 學務處 and 輔導室 cannot refuse a request for help, and this is exactly what that provision is for.

questions.stem: You have a genuine suspicion that a child in your class is being harmed at home. What is the deadline for reporting it?
options: Immediately, and in any case no later than 24 hours
As soon as you have collected enough evidence
Within one school week
At the next staff meeting
questions.why: Both the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act (Art. 53) and the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Art. 50) use the same wording: immediately, and no later than 24 hours. There is no version of this rule that lets you wait and see.

src.label: Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act, Art. 53 →

questions.stem: What standard must be met before you are required to report?
options: You must be certain the abuse happened
You must have physical evidence
You must have a reasonable suspicion
The child must ask you to report it
questions.why: The threshold is suspicion, not certainty. Weighing evidence is the job of social services and the school's designated staff — and quietly deciding for yourself that it is “probably nothing” is the single most common reason a report never gets made.

questions.stem: When does the 24-hour clock start?
options: When you personally decide the case is serious
When the report reaches the county government
When the first member of staff becomes aware — everyone who knows shares the same 24 hours
When the school principal is informed
questions.why: The clock runs from the first staff member's knowledge, and it is shared by everyone who knows. Passing the information to a colleague does not reset it. That is why “I told my co-teacher and assumed she'd handle it” is not a safe answer.

questions.stem: A student shows you bruises. What is your role?
options: Tell the designated person; you are not the investigator
Ask the child detailed questions to establish what happened
Photograph the injuries as evidence
Investigate carefully so your report is accurate
questions.why: You report; you do not investigate. Your own inquiries can contaminate a professional investigation and can make a child's later account less usable. Photographing a child's body is not yours to do and creates its own problems.

questions.stem: A child begins telling you something upsetting and says: “Promise you won't tell anyone.” The right response is:
options: Stop the conversation immediately and walk away
Say nothing and let the child keep talking
Promise, so the child feels safe enough to continue
Say honestly that you must tell one person whose job it is to help, and tell the child who that is
questions.why: A promise you cannot keep is a betrayal the child will feel later, and it damages their trust in every adult after you. Being honest in the moment — “I have to tell one person, and I'll tell you who” — keeps you truthful without shutting the child down. Then stay, and listen without questioning.

questions.stem: Before reporting a suspected case of abuse at home, should you contact the child's parents to check?
options: Yes — parents deserve to hear it from the school first
No — never contact the family first
Yes, but only through the homeroom teacher
Only if the child agrees
questions.why: Never. In a significant share of cases the person you would be warning is the person causing the harm, and warning them puts the child at greater risk and destroys any chance of a clean investigation. Family contact is a decision for social services and the school's designated staff, not for you.

questions.stem: You raise a concern with your co-teacher. She says: “Let's wait — I'll talk to the homeroom teacher tomorrow and we'll decide then.” What should you do?
options: Accept her judgment; she knows the family and the system better
Make sure the report is made today — go to the designated person yourself if needed
Wait 24 hours and then follow up
Let it go; raising it once discharges your duty
questions.why: The duty is personal and the clock is already running. Your co-teacher's seniority does not transfer your obligation to her, and “we'll decide tomorrow” is exactly how a 24-hour deadline gets missed. Do it without drama: tell her you are going to pass it on today because of the time limit. That framing is factual, not an accusation.

questions.stem: Which of these makes a mandatory report unnecessary?
options: The child says they fell down the stairs
The family is known to the school and considered respectable
Another teacher says the child exaggerates
None of these
questions.why: None of them. Children very often explain injuries in ways that protect the adult harming them, reputations tell you nothing, and second-hand character assessments are not evidence. Every one of these is a familiar reason a report was not filed — which is precisely why the legal threshold is suspicion and the decision is not left to you.

questions.stem: Under Article 53, what protection does the person making the report have?
options: None — the report is public record
The reporter's identity is kept confidential by law
Protection only if the report turns out to be correct
Protection only for Taiwanese nationals
questions.why: Article 53 makes the reporter's identity confidential by law. And a report made in good faith that turns out to be mistaken is not a problem — that outcome is designed into the system. A report never made is the failure the law is aimed at.

questions.stem: An educator who fails to report without justification faces:
options: An administrative fine
A verbal warning only
Immediate deportation
Nothing; the duty is advisory
questions.why: Failure to report without legitimate cause carries a fine of NT$6,000–60,000 under Art. 100 of the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act, and NT$6,000–30,000 under Art. 62 of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act. The penalty is not the real reason to report — but it does tell you how seriously the system treats this.

questions.stem: It is a Saturday. You have a serious concern and cannot reach anyone at your school. What do you do?
options: Wait until Monday morning
Post in the school LINE group
Contact the parents yourself
Call 113, the Protection Hotline — 24 hours, English available
questions.why: 113 operates 24 hours with English available, and you can also file online through 關懷e起來 (ecare.mohw.gov.tw) at any time. If a child is in immediate physical danger, call 110 first. “The office was closed” is not a justification for missing the deadline.

questions.stem: Who is allowed to make a child-protection report?
options: Anyone at all — the law expressly permits any person to report
Only the school, acting as an institution
Only a Taiwanese citizen
Only mandated professionals such as teachers, doctors and police
questions.why: Article 53 requires certain professionals to report and separately permits anyone to report. That second paragraph matters to you: if you have told the school and you are not confident anything happened, you can still make the report yourself. Nobody's permission is needed.

questions.stem: After a child discloses something to you, what should you write down?
options: Nothing — written notes can be used against you
Your assessment of whether the child is telling the truth
The date, time, place, and the child's words as closely as you can recall them
A summary in your own words, interpreting what they meant
questions.why: Record facts, not conclusions: when, where, who was present, and what the child actually said — their words, not your paraphrase. Do it as soon as you are alone, while it is fresh. Your interpretation is not useful to an investigation and can actively distort it.

questions.stem: A student tells you they have been cutting themselves and asks you not to tell anyone. What do you do?
options: Keep the confidence to preserve their trust
Tell 輔導室 immediately and do not leave the student alone
Wait and watch for a few days
Tell the class homeroom teacher at the end of term
questions.why: Do not leave them alone, do not promise secrecy, and get 輔導室 (Counseling) involved immediately — walk them there yourself if you can. This is also reportable through the campus safety system. The 24-hour framing applies, but the practical answer is “now”, not “today”.

questions.stem: Which number is Taiwan's 24-hour Protection Hotline for child abuse, domestic violence and sexual assault?
questions.why: 113. English is available. Save it now, alongside 110 (police), 119 (fire and ambulance) and 1990 (Foreigners in Taiwan hotline).

questions.stem: For educators in Taiwan, reporting suspected child abuse is:
options: A professional courtesy
A legal duty set out in statute
Optional for teachers who are not Taiwanese nationals
A school policy that varies between schools
questions.why: It is a statutory duty. Article 53 of the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act names educators specifically, and Article 50 of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act does the same. Your school will treat you as carrying this duty — and the right action is the same either way.

questions.stem: What you saw does not fit neatly into any of the listed categories of harm. What does that mean?
options: You should ask the child which category applies
You should wait until it fits a category
No report is required
The law includes a general “any other harm” category — report it
questions.why: Article 53 ends with a deliberate catch-all covering any other circumstance of harm. It exists precisely so that “it didn't quite fit the list” can never be the reason a child went unreported. If you are worried, that is enough to pass it on.

questions.stem: A child starts telling you something serious. Which response is best in the moment?
options: Ask detailed follow-up questions so you have the full picture
Listen without questioning, thank them, and tell them what happens next
Bring another teacher over immediately so the child can repeat it
Suggest they write it down instead
questions.why: Listen; do not interview. Repeated questioning — and being made to repeat a disclosure to a second adult — is harmful to the child and weakens the account for the people who will investigate properly. Your job in the room is to stay calm, listen, and be honest about the next step.

questions.stem: Who at your school should receive your report first?
options: The principal, always
Whichever colleague you know best
The county Education Department
The designated person named in your school's prevention rules — usually 學務處 or 輔導室
questions.why: Every school names designated staff in its own prevention rules; in most schools that is 學務處 (Student Affairs) or 輔導室 (Counseling). They file both the campus-safety report and the social-services report. Find out the name and extension at your school before you ever need it.

questions.stem: You report a concern to your co-teacher, who is senior to you and knows the family. She says: “I know this family. It's not what you think. Leave it with me.” Two days later nothing appears to have happened. What is the correct action?
options: Report it yourself now, to the designated person or via 113 / 關懷e起來, and tell her you have done so
Raise it again with her and give her another week
Take it straight to the county Education Department
Trust her judgment — she has the context you lack
questions.why: The duty is personal and the deadline has already passed. Anyone may file a report, so nothing is blocking you. Telling her you have done it — plainly, without accusation — is better than doing it behind her back: it keeps the working relationship survivable and makes clear you acted on a legal obligation rather than on distrust of her.

questions.stem: You made a report six weeks ago. Nobody has told you anything since, and the child seems unchanged. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing — confidentiality means you are usually not told the outcome, and no news is not evidence of no action
The report was probably dismissed as unfounded
You should re-report the identical concern weekly
You should ask the child directly what happened
questions.why: You are generally not entitled to case information, and silence tells you nothing about what is happening. What you should do is keep reporting anything new — each fresh concern is its own report — and keep your own dated notes. Asking the child what social services did is not appropriate.

questions.stem: A parent confronts you angrily, having worked out that a report about their family came from your class. The best response is:
options: Deny that you made any report
Explain your reasoning and the evidence you had

Say that you are legally required to pass on any concern about a child, that you cannot discuss an individual case, and refer them to the school — then tell your principal about the confrontation the same day
Apologize and say you will not do it again
questions.why: Do not litigate the case at the school gate and do not disclose details. State the duty in general terms, decline to discuss specifics, and disengage. Then inform your principal and Personnel the same day — an angry parent contact should reach school leadership from you first, not from the parent. Your identity as reporter is protected by law, and your school should be protecting you here.

questions.stem: You are genuinely unsure whether what you noticed is serious enough to report. Which reasoning is correct?
options: Uncertainty means you should observe for another week before deciding
You should consult two colleagues and follow the majority view
You should report only if you would be willing to testify
Uncertainty is exactly the situation the low threshold is designed for — report it
questions.why: The threshold is suspicion precisely so that uncertain cases still reach the people trained to assess them. “I'll watch for another week” is the single most common failure mode, and it is the one the deadline exists to prevent. A good-faith report that turns out to be wrong costs nothing; the reverse error costs a child.

questions.stem: During a lesson, a student mentions something that suggests a member of school staff — not a family member — may be harming a child. What changes?
options: You should wait and gather corroboration from other students
You should raise it privately with that colleague first
Nothing changes; report it exactly as you would any other concern
You should say nothing without proof, because an accusation could end a career
questions.why: The duty is the same and so is the deadline — reporting is not an accusation, it is a referral to people whose job it is to determine what happened. Never warn the person concerned, and never canvass other students; both destroy an investigation. If the concern involves the school's own leadership, the case goes to the county education authority rather than being handled internally. Where the conduct is sexual or gender-related, Module 5 covers the separate procedure and its much larger penalties.

questions.stem: You become aware of a suspected campus gender incident. What is the reporting deadline under the Gender Equity Education Act?
options: Before the end of the semester
48 hours
One school week
24 hours
questions.why: Article 22: a principal, teacher, staff member or worker who becomes aware of a suspected campus gender incident must report to the school's designated staff, no later than 24 hours. Same deadline as child protection, and the clock likewise starts with the first staff member who knows.

questions.stem: For an incident to be a “campus gender incident”, one party must be a principal, teacher, staff member, worker or student. What must the other party be?
options: Any adult connected to the school
A student
A member of staff
A parent or guardian
questions.why: Article 3: the other party must be a student. This is what defines the category — and it is also why, if you are the one being harassed, this is not the route that protects you. See the last section of the briefing.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the four types of campus gender incident?
options: A disagreement between two teachers about gender-neutral language
Sexual bullying
Sexual harassment
A staff member's sex- or gender-related breach of professional ethics
questions.why: The four types are sexual assault, sexual harassment, sexual bullying, and — added in the 2023 amendment — sex- or gender-related conduct by a principal or staff member that violates professional ethics. That fourth category is deliberately broader than harassment: conduct can breach professional ethics without meeting the harassment threshold.

questions.stem: An educator who fails to report a suspected campus gender incident within 24 hours, without legitimate cause, faces a fine of:
options: No fine; the duty is advisory
questions.why: Article 43: NT$30,000–150,000 — five times the child-protection penalty, and the largest in this series. The same fine applies to forging, altering, destroying or concealing evidence of such an incident. That last clause is worth remembering: deleting a message thread after the fact is itself a penalised act.

questions.stem: After a report is made, who investigates?
options: The homeroom teacher and the parents
The school's Gender Equity Education Committee (性平會), or the competent authority
The teacher who received the disclosure
The police, in every case
questions.why: The 性平會 investigates, and must complete within two months under Article 36 (extendable twice by one month each). Your role ends at reporting. Conducting your own inquiry — asking other students, confronting the person named — contaminates the investigation and can itself become a finding against you.

questions.stem: A student describes something a colleague did that sounds like harassment. Your colleague is popular and has taught for twenty years. What is the correct action?
options: Speak to the colleague privately first to hear their side
Ask other students whether they have experienced the same
Report it within 24 hours, exactly as you would any other case
Wait to see whether the student mentions it again
questions.why: Reporting is a referral, not an accusation — the whole point is that someone else determines what happened. Warning the person concerned and canvassing other students are the two actions most likely to destroy an investigation, and both can be treated as concealing or contaminating evidence. Seniority and reputation are not exceptions written into Article 22.

questions.stem: You think what you overheard was “probably just a joke between friends.” What does that change?
options: Nothing — the threshold is suspicion, and assessing it is not your job
It removes the duty, since no harm was intended
It means you should report it only if it happens again
It means you should ask the students whether they were joking
questions.why: The standard is a suspected incident, and whether conduct was harmful is precisely the question the 性平會 exists to answer. Intent is not the test — how the conduct reasonably appeared and how it affected the student is. “I assumed it was a joke” is a very common opening line in cases that turned out not to be.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old student asks to add you on Instagram. The right answer is:
options: Accept, but only if your account is set to private
Decline, and keep student communication in school channels
Accept and mute them
Accept — refusing damages your relationship with the class
questions.why: Private accounts do not help; the issue is the private channel itself, not who else can see it. Decline warmly and generally — “I don't add students, it's the same for everyone” — so it does not read as personal rejection. This single habit prevents more cases involving foreign teachers than any other rule in this module.

questions.stem: A student needs a private conversation with you about a personal matter. Where should it happen?
options: Over private message, so nobody overhears
In an empty classroom with the door closed, for privacy
In your car, where nobody will interrupt
In a visible place — door open, or a corridor or shared space
questions.why: Confidential does not have to mean unwitnessed. Keep the door open, or move somewhere a passer-by can see you both but not hear you. Protecting the student's privacy and protecting yourself from an unverifiable account of what happened are not in conflict — visibility gives you both.

questions.stem: It is raining and a student you know well misses the bus. Should you drive them home?
options: Yes, if you tell the homeroom teacher afterwards
Yes, if the student's parents approve by phone
No — find another solution through the school
Yes, if another student comes along
questions.why: Do not transport a student alone. Take it to 學務處 or the homeroom teacher and let the school solve it — that is a normal request and they will have a normal answer. Kindness that puts you alone and unobserved with a student is the exact pattern this module exists to break.

questions.stem: A second-grade student runs up and hugs you in the corridor. The best response is:
options: Redirect warmly to a high-five, in view of others, without shaming the child
Push them away firmly so the boundary is clear
Hug back — it would be cruel to reject a small child
Report the incident within 24 hours
questions.why: Neither extreme is right. Young children hug; the answer is a warm redirection that keeps the affection and loses the ambiguity — a high-five, a wave, in a place where others can see. Do this consistently from the first week and it stops being a moment at all.

questions.stem: A student who disclosed something to you says: “Please don't tell anyone, I'll deny it.” Can you still report?
options: No — reporting without consent breaks the student's trust
Yes — you must report; the duty does not depend on the student's consent
Only if another teacher witnessed it
No — a report needs the student's written statement
questions.why: The duty is yours and does not depend on consent, and this is exactly why you never promise secrecy in the first place. What you can offer is honesty and control over the small things: tell them who you must tell, what will likely happen next, and that you will stay alongside them through it.

questions.stem: A colleague repeatedly makes remarks about your body and appearance. Which statement is correct?
options: Foreign contract teachers are not covered by any harassment protection
Nothing can be done unless there is a witness
This is a campus gender incident and goes to the 性平會 like any other
The campus gender incident route does not cover it, because the other party must be a student — your protection comes through your employer, so go to 人事室 and the principal
questions.why: A campus gender incident requires the other party to be a student, so this is a workplace matter, not that route. Your employer has obligations to you: go to 人事室 and the principal, ask what procedure applies, and ask for the answer in writing. If the school does not act, the county Education Department and the labour authority are both open to you, and 1990 will point you to the right office in English. Raising it is your right and is not a threat to your contract.

questions.stem: After hearing about a possible incident, you delete an old LINE thread that you think might be misread. This is:
options: Sensible — you are protecting your privacy
Neutral; the messages were unrelated
A separately penalised act — concealing or destroying evidence carries the same NT$30,000–150,000 fine
Fine, as long as the other person still has a copy
questions.why: Article 43 penalises forging, altering, destroying or concealing evidence at the same level as failing to report. However bad an old message looks, deleting it looks incomparably worse and converts an explainable situation into an unexplainable one. Preserve everything, and say plainly that you are worried about how something reads.

questions.stem: Which Act governs campus gender incidents in Taiwanese schools?
options: The Gender Equity Education Act 性別平等教育法
The Employment Service Act
The Teachers' Act
The Domestic Violence Prevention Act
questions.why: The Gender Equity Education Act (性別平等教育法), last amended 16 August 2023. An official English translation is on the Laws & Regulations Database — worth ten minutes of your time, because it is the statute in this series most likely to affect you directly.

questions.stem: What is the 性平會?
options: A parents' association
A teachers' union
The school's Gender Equity Education Committee, which investigates campus gender incidents
A county-level appeals court
questions.why: The Gender Equity Education Committee. Every school has one. It receives cases, investigates, and reports its findings — within two months under Article 36. Knowing it exists, and that it is separate from the ordinary school hierarchy, is the point.

questions.stem: Do you need to be sure an incident occurred before you report it?
options: Yes — reporting an unconfirmed suspicion is defamatory
No — the duty is triggered by a suspected incident
Only if the student is under 12
Only if there is physical evidence
questions.why: Article 22 says suspected. Determining what actually happened is the 性平會's job, not yours — and a report is a referral, not an accusation. Trying to be sure first is how the 24-hour deadline gets missed.

questions.stem: Which of these is acceptable practice?
options: Meeting a student in a public, visible space with the door open
Tutoring one student alone in a room with the door closed
Adding a student on a personal social media account
Driving a student home alone after a late activity
questions.why: Visibility is the whole principle. Closed doors, private channels and cars all share one feature — no third party can ever say what happened. Keep the conversation, lose the ambiguity.

questions.stem: A student has clearly lost weight over the holidays and you want to say something kind. What should you do?
options: Compliment them on how good they look
Ask privately whether they have been dieting
Mention it lightly in front of the class so it is not awkward
Say nothing about their body; if you are concerned, tell 輔導室
questions.why: Remarks about a student's body are off-limits even as compliments — praise for weight loss is well documented as harmful where an eating disorder is developing, and it is not information you have. If you are worried, that concern belongs with 輔導室, who are trained for it.

questions.stem: A student discloses something about another teacher, then panics: “Please forget I said it. I'll say I made it up.” You are certain that going ahead will cost you the student's trust. What do you do?
options: Report within 24 hours, and be honest with the student about what you are doing and why
Tell the student to speak to the 輔導室 themselves
Wait a week to see whether the student raises it again
Respect the student's wishes; a broken trust does more harm
questions.why: The duty does not turn on consent, and this is why you never promise secrecy. What you can control is how it is done: tell the student who you must tell, what is likely to happen, and that you are not disappearing. Handled that way, most students do not experience it as betrayal — and passing the decision back to a frightened child is not a kindness.

questions.stem: You raise a concern about a colleague's behavior toward students. Your co-teacher says: “He's like that with everyone. It's just his personality — don't make trouble.” What is the correct action?
options: Keep observing until you have a clearer example
Defer to her reading; she knows him and the school
Report it within 24 hours anyway, and tell her you are doing so because the law gives you no discretion
Raise it informally with the colleague himself
questions.why: “He's like that with everyone” describes a pattern, not an exception. The obligation is personal and the clock is already running, so a colleague's reassurance cannot discharge it. Saying openly that you have no discretion here is both true and the least damaging framing available — it moves the conversation from your judgment of him to the statute's requirement of you.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old student has developed an obvious crush and starts sending you affectionate messages through a school platform. What is the right response?
options: Reply kindly but firmly in private, and handle it discreetly yourself
Ask another student to tell them to stop
Ignore the messages and hope it passes
Preserve the messages, stop replying beyond a short neutral acknowledgement, and tell your co-teacher and 輔導室 the same day
questions.why: Handling it privately is the instinct that turns a manageable situation into a case — because the only record left is a private exchange you managed alone. Preserve everything, keep any reply short and neutral, and bring it to your co-teacher and 輔導室 immediately. Reporting it early protects the student as well as you: it is not a punishment, and it means the adults around them can respond well.

questions.stem: Reviewing old messages, you find something you wrote months ago that was meant warmly but could easily be read the wrong way. What should you do?
options: Delete it — nobody has seen it and no case exists
Leave it and say nothing unless asked
Preserve it, and raise it yourself with your principal or 人事室, explaining the context now
Ask the student to delete their copy too
questions.why: Deleting it is a separately penalised act if an incident is ever alleged, and asking a student to delete their copy is far worse — that is direct evidence tampering involving a child. Raising it yourself, before anyone asks, is the strongest position you will ever be in: context volunteered early reads as candour, and the same context offered under investigation reads as defense.

questions.stem: The concern you need to report is about the school principal. Where does the case go?
options: To the principal, as the head of the school
To the school's 性平會, as with any other case
Nowhere; a principal can only be investigated by the police
To the county education authority — a school cannot handle a case about its own head
questions.why: A school cannot receive and investigate a case about its own leadership — the case goes to the competent authority above it, in your case the Changhua County Education Department. The 2023 amendment tightened these recusal rules considerably. If you are ever in this position, put your report in writing, keep a dated copy, and consider calling 1990 for guidance in English before you file.

questions.stem: You suspect a student in your class is being bullied. What is the reporting deadline?
options: As soon as you can confirm it
One school week
48 hours
24 hours
questions.why: Article 17 of the 校園霸凌防制準則: principals and staff who become aware of a suspected campus bullying incident must report immediately to the school's designated person, and in no case later than 24 hours. This is the third module in this series with the same clock — child protection, gender incidents, bullying.

src.label: 校園霸凌防制準則, Art. 17 →

questions.stem: Which element most clearly separates bullying from an ordinary conflict between students?
options: Whether an injury resulted
Whether it is persistent rather than a one-off
Whether a teacher witnessed it
Whether the parents complained
questions.why: Persistence (持續) is written into the definition in Article 4. A single fight is a discipline matter, not bullying. A pattern sustained over weeks is exactly what the regulation targets — which is why what you notice over time is worth more to a case than any single dramatic incident.

questions.stem: Students are attacking a classmate in a LINE group outside school hours. Is this within scope?
options: No — it happened outside school
No — the regulation covers physical conduct only
Yes — electronic communication and the internet are named in the definition
Only if the school's own network was used
questions.why: The definition expressly lists electronic communication and the internet among the means, alongside speech, writing, pictures, symbols and physical acts. Campus bullying also covers conduct occurring outside the campus. Online is not an edge case here — it is written into the text.

questions.stem: A student is never physically touched, but is consistently excluded — nobody will pair with them, and a group organizes to leave them out. Is this bullying?
options: Yes — excluding is listed conduct, and indirect acts are covered
No, because exclusion is a normal part of childhood
Only if the student says they are upset
No, because there is no physical contact
questions.why: Excluding (排擠) is named conduct, and the definition covers indirect as well as direct acts. The test is whether the person is placed in a hostile or unfriendly environment — not whether they were injured and not whether they cried. This form is also the hardest to see, which is why a teacher who watches pair-forming has genuine value.

questions.stem: After you report, whose job is it to establish what happened?
options: The homeroom teacher's
The school's process — a review sub-group decides whether to accept the case, then a handling team runs 調和 or a formal investigation
Yours, since you saw it
The parents', by agreement between the families
questions.why: The 2024 framework is deliberately structured: a prevention committee with a review sub-group to decide acceptance, then a handling team to conduct facilitated dialogue or an investigation and report back. Your own inquiries — asking the class who saw what, collecting statements — damage that process and can breach confidentiality before it opens.

questions.stem: You decide to sit the two students down yourself and get them to talk it out. This is:
options: A good first step before involving anyone else
Inappropriate — 調和 is a formal process run by the handling team, with consent requirements
Fine if both students agree
Required before a report can be made
questions.why: Facilitated dialogue (調和) is a formal procedure run by a neutral handling team, not a small version of a chat you host. Doing it informally can leave a target feeling pressured to forgive someone who is still hurting them, and it compromises the real process before it begins.

questions.stem: 調和 (facilitated dialogue) can be used:
options: In any bullying case, at the school's discretion
Only after an investigation has concluded
Only where the parents request it
Only in student-to-student cases, and only if both parties consent
questions.why: It applies to student-to-student cases and requires the agreement of both the person who acted and the person affected. It cannot be imposed — which is the safeguard that stops a restorative process from becoming a way of quietly closing a case.

questions.stem: The conduct you have observed appears to be sexual bullying. Where does the case go?
options: Through the bullying prevention committee as normal
To the Gender Equity Education Act procedure instead
To the police
Nowhere — sexual conduct between students is not covered
questions.why: Article 4 routes conduct amounting to sexual bullying out of this regulation and into the Gender Equity Education Act — Module 5's procedure, and Module 5's much larger penalties. You are not expected to make that call: report within 24 hours and let the school route it. Knowing the two tracks exist just stops you concluding it “isn't really bullying”.

questions.stem: A concern involves a member of staff behaving this way toward a student, rather than another student. What changes?
options: It follows a different procedure, but your duty to report within 24 hours is unchanged
Nothing — the same committee handles it
It cannot be reported by another teacher
It must go directly to the police
questions.why: Staff-to-student cases run through the process governing teacher discipline rather than the bullying committee. Your obligation does not change at all: report to the designated person within 24 hours. Never raise it with the colleague first, and never canvass students — both destroy an investigation.

questions.stem: You are interviewed as a witness in a bullying investigation. Which is true?
options: You should record the interview yourself for your own protection
No recording is made of witness interviews
The school records the interview in full; those being interviewed may not record on their own
You may bring a friend to record it
questions.why: Article 39 requires the school to make a full audio or video recording of interviews, and expressly prohibits interviewees from recording themselves. If you are called as a witness, expect this and do not attempt your own recording — doing so is a breach in itself.

questions.stem: What are your obligations regarding confidentiality once a case is under way?
options: You may discuss it with colleagues who teach the same class
You may discuss it if you avoid using names
Confidentiality applies only to the investigation team
You must not disclose identifying information at all — leaking can be punished under the Criminal Code or other law
questions.why: Article 40 makes the duty binding and backs it with criminal liability. In a school where everyone knows every class, “no names” protects nobody. That means not telling the class, not telling other parents, not discussing it in the staff room, and not posting about it — including in the abstract.

questions.stem: You want the class to know this behavior is unacceptable, so you say: “Some people in this class need to start being kinder.” This is:
options: An effective preventive intervention
Acceptable if no names are used
Required as part of prevention education
Unhelpful — it signals to the target that you know and are not acting, and tells everyone else who it is about
questions.why: Everyone in the room decodes it instantly, including the target — who learns that an adult knows and has responded with a vague remark. Anti-bullying messages belong in planned lessons and in the school's prevention program. Responses to an actual incident belong in a report and in the things you change.

questions.stem: While the school's process runs, what is genuinely within your control?
options: Speaking to both sets of parents
Nothing — you must not interfere in any way
Seating, grouping, and assigning pairs rather than letting students choose
Moving the target to a different class
questions.why: You control your room. Assigning pairs rather than letting students self-select is not a minor adjustment: for a child who is never chosen, it is the difference between a lesson they dread and a lesson they can sit through. It also requires no permission, breaches no confidentiality, and can start in your next lesson.

questions.stem: What kind of record is most useful to a bullying investigation?
options: Your assessment of which student is at fault
Statements collected from other students
Dated, factual notes on what you observed over a period of weeks
Photographs of the students involved
questions.why: Persistence is the element the definition turns on, so a series of small dated entries evidences it far better than one dramatic account. Record what you saw and heard, not your conclusions about who is to blame — and do not gather statements from students, which is investigating.

questions.stem: Campus bullying (校園霸凌) covers conduct occurring:
options: Both inside and outside the campus
During school hours only
Inside the school grounds only
Only where a teacher was present
questions.why: The definition covers bullying by school staff or students against students, occurring inside or outside the campus. Combined with the express inclusion of the internet, that means a group chat at 10 p.m. on a Sunday is squarely within scope.

questions.stem: Who should receive your report first?
options: The school's designated person, who then reports to the competent authority
The police
The parents of the student affected
The county Education Department
questions.why: Article 17 sets the chain: staff report to the school's designated person, who reports upward to the competent authority — the whole chain within 24 hours. Find out who that person is at your school before you need them, exactly as in Module 4.

questions.stem: Does the student have to be physically injured for it to be bullying?
options: Yes, unless the conduct occurred online
Yes — some harm must be demonstrable
Only for cases involving younger students
No — the test is whether they are placed in a hostile or unfriendly environment
questions.why: The definition ends on the effect: placing the person in a hostile or unfriendly environment. Injury is not required, and neither is a visible reaction. Many targets work very hard at showing nothing at all.

questions.stem: A student tells you that someone else — not them — is being bullied. What do you do?
options: Ask the student for more details first so your report is complete
Report it within 24 hours, exactly as if you had seen it
Suggest the student tell the homeroom teacher themselves
Wait to see whether you observe it yourself
questions.why: The duty is triggered by becoming aware of a suspected incident, however you became aware. Do not interview the student for detail — that is investigating. Thank them, tell them you have to pass it on, and pass it on. A student who reports and sees nothing happen does not report again.

questions.stem: The students involved say they were “only joking.” How does that affect the analysis?
options: It ends the matter — bullying requires intent to harm
It halves the seriousness of the case
It does not resolve it: teasing is listed conduct, and the test is the effect on the other person
It matters only if a teacher witnessed the exchange
questions.why: The conduct must be deliberate, but teasing (戲弄) is expressly listed among the named behaviors, and the definition turns on whether the other person is left in a hostile or unfriendly environment. “We were only joking” is the most common thing said in these cases and settles nothing — which is precisely why the assessment is not left to you.

questions.stem: Over six weeks you have watched one student consistently left out, spoken over and quietly mocked. There is no single incident you could point to. What should you do?
options: Keep observing until you have one clear incident to report
Mention it informally to the homeroom teacher and leave it there
Raise it with the students involved directly
Report the pattern now, with your dated notes — persistence is the element the definition turns on
questions.why: Waiting for a single dramatic incident misunderstands the definition: the pattern is the case. Six weeks of dated observations evidence persistence in a way one incident never could, and they are exactly what a handling team cannot reconstruct on its own. This is also the situation in which a foreign teacher's view of a class is genuinely irreplaceable.

questions.stem: The student being targeted begs you not to report it: “It'll get so much worse if you do.” What is the right response?
options: Report it, tell them honestly that you have to and what will happen next, and change what you control in your own lesson immediately
Respect their wish; they understand the situation better than you
Agree to wait two weeks and review
Ask them to tell 輔導室 themselves
questions.why: The duty is not conditional on consent, and this fear is usually well founded — which is a reason to make the report carefully, not to skip it. Be honest about what you must do, tell them who will know, ask 輔導室 what support they will get, and change seating and grouping in your room the same week so that something visibly improves rather than only becoming more official.

questions.stem: You raise it with your co-teacher, who says: “They're children. They'll sort it out among themselves.” What should you do?
options: Report it within 24 hours anyway, and tell her you are doing so because the regulation gives you no discretion
Defer to her; she knows these students far better than you
Keep observing and raise it again in a month
Take it straight to the principal
questions.why: Her reading may even be right about these particular children — but Article 17 does not give either of you the discretion to make that call, and the clock is already running. Framing it as “the rule gives me no choice” rather than “I disagree with you” is both true and the version of this conversation that leaves the working relationship intact.

questions.stem: A parent asks you what is happening in a bullying case involving their child's class. You know some of it. What do you say?
options: Share what you know, since the parent has a legitimate interest
Share it without using names
Say that you cannot discuss it and that the school is the right place to ask — then tell your principal about the approach the same day
Say you know nothing about any case
questions.why: Confidentiality is legally binding and backed by criminal liability, and omitting names protects nobody in a school where everyone knows every class. Decline, redirect to the school, and tell your principal the same day — leadership should hear about a parent approach from you first, not later from the parent.

questions.stem: You reported a case a month ago. Nothing visible has changed, and the target tells you it is still happening. What is the correct action?
options: Accept that the process has run and the school has decided
Report the new incidents — each fresh incident is its own report, on its own 24-hour clock
Confront the students responsible yourself
Advise the family to make a formal complaint
questions.why: You are generally not told the outcome, so silence tells you nothing about what has happened. What continues to be yours is the new information: each fresh incident is a fresh report with its own deadline. Keep the dated log running, ask 輔導室 what support the target is receiving, and keep changing what you control in your own room.

questions.stem: Parents signed the school's image consent form at the start of the year. You post a photo of your class on your personal Instagram. Is that covered?
options: Yes — consent was given for photographs of the students
Yes, as long as you do not name anyone
No — the consent covers the school's stated purposes, not your personal account
Yes, if the account is private
questions.why: Personal data may be used within the necessary scope of the specific purpose families were told about. That purpose is the school's, not yours. “No names” and “private account” do not convert an outside-purpose use into an inside-purpose one — and you have not read the form, so you do not actually know what it says.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act?
options: A student's photograph
A grammar worksheet you wrote yourself
A student's family circumstances
A student's grades
questions.why: Names, photographs, grades, health information, counseling records and family circumstances are all personal data about an identifiable person. Your own worksheet is your work — a copyright question, not a privacy one.

questions.stem: You want to photocopy two pages from a published textbook for your class. Under the Copyright Act this is:
options: Generally permitted — Article 46 allows reproduction within a reasonable scope for school teaching
Permitted only for material more than ten years old
Prohibited without the publisher's written license
Permitted only if you credit the author on every page
questions.why: Article 46 allows a school and its teaching staff to reproduce published works within a reasonable scope for the needs of school teaching. “Reasonable” is doing real work in that sentence — a couple of pages for your lesson, not a whole book, and not a substitute for buying the class set.

questions.stem: You then upload the same two pages to your public teaching blog so other teachers can use them. This is:
options: Also covered by Article 46, since the purpose is still educational
Not covered — public transmission is a separate right that classroom fair use does not reach
Fine because the blog earns no money
Fine if you add a note saying it is for educational use
questions.why: This is the single most useful distinction in the module: legal in your classroom does not mean legal on the internet. Uploading is 公開傳輸 (public transmission), a separate right, and the teaching exceptions are written around the needs of a class — not around distribution to the world. Non-commercial and well-intentioned do not change the analysis.

questions.stem: A parent messages you directly asking how their child is doing. The best response is:
options: Reply briefly and politely, redirect substantive matters to the homeroom teacher, and tell your co-teacher that the contact happened
Do not reply at all
Give a full account — parents are entitled to know
Reply only if the homeroom teacher approves each message
questions.why: Warmth costs nothing and silence reads as rudeness, but the 導師 is the school's channel to families and holds the full picture. Telling your co-teacher matters as much as the reply itself: they should never learn about a parent contact from the parent.

questions.stem: At a parent meeting, one parent asks about a different child in the class who has been having problems. You should:
options: Answer generally without using the child's name
Decline to discuss another family's child at all
Answer only if the other child's parent is not present
Redirect the question to the homeroom teacher and then answer briefly
questions.why: There is no version of this that is acceptable, including the careful-sounding ones. In a class of thirty, “a child who has been struggling recently” identifies someone to everyone in the room. Decline, kindly and without explanation.

questions.stem: Which of these ways of returning test results is appropriate?
options: Handing papers back face-down, or individually
Posting a ranked list on the classroom wall
Reading scores aloud in class order
Asking students to swap and mark each other's, then announce
questions.why: A student's grades are personal data, and a classroom is a public place. Face-down or individual return costs you nothing. Public ranking is also poor teaching quite apart from the privacy question — see Module 3 on punishment tied to academic results.

questions.stem: A student produces a wonderful poster. You want to put a photo of it on your public blog. What matters?
options: Nothing — you set the task, so the work is yours
Only whether the student's name is visible
Only whether the school logo is visible
The work belongs to the student — ask before displaying it publicly, and consider the privacy question separately
questions.why: Two separate issues, both real. Copyright in a student's own work belongs to the student, so displaying it publicly is a permission question. And if their name or handwriting or face appears, the privacy analysis runs in parallel. Asking the student — and the school — takes a minute.

questions.stem: You are leaving Taiwan and want to keep your photographs of the students as a memento. The right thing to do is:
options: Delete them — they were collected for a purpose that ends with the job
Keep only the ones where faces are unclear
Keep them privately; you will never post them
Ask each student individually for permission to keep them
questions.why: The images exist because of the role, and the role is ending. Keeping a private archive of identifiable children from a job you have left is difficult to justify to anyone who asks later, and impossible to justify to a family. Take photographs of the school gate, the staff room, your colleagues instead — those are yours.

questions.stem: A parent asks you to tutor their child privately at weekends, offering good pay. This is:
options: A permit question, not a scheduling question — teaching outside your permitted employment needs separate authorization
Fine, since it is outside school hours
Fine if the principal knows
Fine if you do not charge
questions.why: Straight back to Module 1: your permission to work is tied to your employer, and your principal cannot widen it. Decline warmly and generally — “I'm not able to teach outside school, it's the same for everyone” — so it does not read as a judgment about that family.

questions.stem: In a staff LINE group you write: “Xiao-Ming really struggled again today, I think something's going on at home.” This is:
options: Fine — it is an internal staff channel
Poor practice — named speculation about a child's home life should go to the homeroom teacher or 輔導室, not a group chat
Fine because you are raising a genuine concern
Fine as long as no parents are in the group
questions.why: The concern is right and the channel is wrong. Group chats are forwarded, screenshotted, and read by people who joined later. Say it to the homeroom teacher or 輔導室 directly — and if you suspect actual harm, Module 4's 24-hour duty applies and a group chat is certainly not the route.

questions.stem: You want to show a short YouTube clip in your lesson, then post your own recording of the lesson online. Which part is the problem?
options: Both are problems
Posting the recording online, because it redistributes the clip
Showing the clip in class
Neither is a problem
questions.why: Playing material in class for teaching purposes is generally within scope. Posting a recording that contains it is redistribution — and if students are visible or audible, you have added a privacy question on top of the copyright one. The lesson is the permitted setting; the upload is a different act.

questions.stem: At a dinner, someone you have just met asks which school you teach at and about the students there. The safest habit is:
options: Answer nothing at all and change the subject
Answer fully; it is public information
Name the school but talk about students only in general terms
Answer only if they are also a teacher
questions.why: Your workplace is not a secret and refusing to say where you work is strange. What does not travel is anything about identifiable children — no stories about a particular student, however funny or moving, told to people who can work out which school and which class.

questions.stem: You realize a post from six months ago includes a clearly identifiable student. What should you do?
options: Leave it; removing it now would draw attention
Delete it quietly and say nothing
Take it down first, then tell your co-teacher or principal the same day
Ask the student's parents directly whether they mind
questions.why: Remove it, then report it — in that order, the same day. A post taken down by the person who posted it and disclosed voluntarily is an ordinary correction. The identical post found by a parent later is an incident, and by then you are explaining rather than telling. Do not contact the family yourself.

questions.stem: Under the Personal Data Protection Act, schools may use student data:
options: For any educational purpose they consider reasonable
However they wish, once consent has been signed once
Only with fresh written consent for every single use
Within the necessary scope of the specific purpose that families were told about
questions.why: Purpose and necessity are the two limits, and families must be told the purpose at the point of collection. Neither “it's educational” nor “they signed something in September” is a general license.

questions.stem: Who is the school's normal channel for communication with families?
options: The English teacher, for anything about English
The Personnel Office
The principal
The homeroom teacher 導師
questions.why: The 導師 holds the relationship, the Chinese and the whole picture of that child. Going around them is not a shortcut — it produces two versions of the school's message and undercuts the person who has to live with the family all year.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest statement of the copyright rule for teachers here?
options: Anything used for education is free to use anywhere
Nothing may be copied without written permission
Copying for your class is generally allowed; putting the same thing on a public website is not
Copyright does not apply to material used in schools
questions.why: Article 46 permits reproduction within a reasonable scope for school teaching. Public transmission — uploading — is a separate right that classroom fair use does not reach. If you remember one sentence from this module, make it this one.

questions.stem: Before posting any photo involving students anywhere outside the school, you should:
options: Check that faces are not clearly visible
Post it and remove it if anyone objects
Check that you have not used any names
Ask your co-teacher or 教務處 first, every time
questions.why: Ask first. The school knows which families have circumstances you will never be told about — a custody dispute, a protection order — and asking is what makes it impossible for you to be the person who caused that harm.

questions.stem: Where should a concern about a particular student's home situation go?
options: The homeroom teacher or 輔導室, directly
A note to the parents
The staff LINE group
Your own diary, until you are sure
questions.why: Direct, named, to the person whose job it is. Group chats get forwarded and screenshotted. And if what you suspect is harm rather than difficulty, Module 4's 24-hour reporting duty applies.

questions.stem: Your school's own Facebook page regularly posts class photos, so you assume the same photos are fine on your personal account. Is that reasoning sound?
options: Yes — the school has clearly established that these photos may be published
Yes, provided you post the identical photos and add nothing
Yes, as long as you tag the school
No — the school publishes under its own consent arrangements and its own responsibility; that does not extend to you
questions.why: The school is the data controller and answers for its own decisions; you are not covered by them. There is also a practical asymmetry worth noticing: the school can take a post down and tell every family it did. You cannot control where an image goes once it leaves your account, and a foreign teacher's account is usually followed by people with no connection to that community at all.

questions.stem: A parent contacts you repeatedly, is warm and complimentary, and gradually starts asking about other students and about staff. The right response is:
options: Block the parent
Answer only the questions about their own child and ignore the rest
Keep the relationship friendly; a supportive parent is an asset
Draw the line explicitly, redirect everything to the homeroom teacher, and tell your co-teacher and principal that this pattern is developing
questions.why: Warmth is exactly how this becomes difficult to refuse — each question is only slightly beyond the last. Quietly ignoring the awkward ones leaves you managing it alone, which is the worst position. Say plainly that you cannot discuss other students or colleagues, move the channel, and make sure the school knows before something is quoted back to you.

questions.stem: You are applying for a job abroad and want to include classroom photos in your portfolio to show your teaching. What is the right approach?
options: Include them; a portfolio is a professional, private document
Include them with faces blurred
Use anonymized descriptions of what you taught, and photograph materials or the room rather than identifiable children
Ask the students to sign a release themselves
questions.why: A portfolio circulates to people with no connection to the school and no accountability to those families, and “private document” describes intent rather than reality. Describe the lesson, show the materials, photograph the empty classroom — that demonstrates your teaching perfectly well. Students cannot consent to this on their own behalf, and asking them puts a child in an impossible position.

questions.stem: A colleague asks you to send them the class photo folder because they are making a farewell video. What should you do?
options: Send it; they are a colleague at the same school
Send only the photos you personally took
Check with 教務處 how such material should be shared and used, rather than deciding it between the two of you
Refuse; the photos are yours
questions.why: A farewell video may well be a normal school activity, properly consented for — that is precisely why the school should be the one saying so. Two teachers agreeing privately is how material ends up somewhere nobody authorized. Ask, and you also find out what the consent form actually covers, which is worth knowing anyway.

questions.stem: A parent tells you their child is being treated unfairly by another teacher and asks what you have observed. You have in fact noticed something. The right response is:
options: Tell them what you saw; the child's welfare comes first
Do not give an account to the parent; take what you observed to the school through the proper route the same day
Suggest the parent make a formal complaint and offer to be a witness
Deny having seen anything
questions.why: Both instincts here are wrong. Feeding a parent an account of a colleague's conduct puts you inside a dispute with no procedure and no protection for anyone — while denying what you saw abandons the child. The observation is real and belongs to the school, today. If what you saw might amount to improper discipline or bullying by staff, Modules 3 and 6 tell you it is reportable in its own right.
